findings.title: Non-atomic match_count update causes lost updates under concurrent requests
findings.body: `should_block?` reads the record, increments `match_count` in Ruby, and then calls `save`. If multiple requests for the same blocked email arrive concurrently (a very plausible scenario since this is specifically meant to catch repeated spam signups), the read-modify-write is not atomic: two processes can read the same `match_count`, each increment it locally, and the last `save` wins, silently losing one of the increments. This makes the match_count/last_match_at statistics unreliable exactly in the high-traffic/spam scenario this feature is designed for. Should use an atomic increment, e.g. `update_counters` or a raw SQL `UPDATE ... SET match_count = match_count + 1`.

findings.title: Validation (and thus BlockedEmail.should_block?) runs twice per signup, double-counting match stats
findings.body: `create` calls `user.valid?` explicitly (to decide whether to call `DiscourseHub.register_nickname`) and then calls `user.save`, which runs full validations again internally. Because `EmailValidator#validate_each` calls `BlockedEmail.should_block?(value)` as a side effect on every validation pass, a single signup attempt against a blocked email will increment `match_count` and update `last_match_at` twice instead of once, corrupting the statistics the feature is meant to track.

findings.title: Blocked-email matching is case-sensitive, allowing trivial bypass
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` looks up `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` with an exact (case-sensitive) match, and the migration (`db/migrate/20130724201552_create_blocked_emails.rb`) creates a case-sensitive unique index on `email`. Nothing in the signup path downcases the submitted email before it reaches this check (unlike `change_email`, which explicitly does `Email.downcase`). A blocked user can bypass the block entirely by altering the case of their email address (e.g. `Spammer@Example.com` instead of `spammer@example.com`), and the uniqueness validation on `BlockedEmail` would also allow two rows that are the same address but differ only in case.

findings.title: Error payload lets clients distinguish 'blocked' from other validation failures, enabling email-blocklist enumeration
findings.body: The `create` action now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` plus the submitted `values`, and the new `user.email.blocked` message ("is not allowed.") is textually distinct from the existing `user.email.not_allowed` message ("is not allowed from that email provider..."). Combined with the JS controller surfacing per-field validation state immediately, this lets an attacker probe arbitrary email addresses against the signup endpoint and determine, based on the returned message, which addresses are present in the `blocked_emails` table versus merely domain-restricted. This creates an oracle for enumerating or testing the blocklist.

findings.title: rejectedEmails array is a shared instance across all controller instances/sessions
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is declared directly on the Ember object literal passed to `extend`, so the array is created once when the class is defined rather than per-instance in `init`. If `CreateAccountController` is ever instantiated more than once (e.g., re-created on route transition, tests, or any code path that doesn't reuse a true singleton), all instances will share and mutate the same array, so rejected emails from one session/user can leak into another and the list is never actually reset. Even for a singleton controller, there is no code path that clears `rejectedEmails`, so once an email is rejected it is permanently flagged invalid client-side for the remainder of the page's life, even if the server-side condition causing the rejection (e.g., a temporarily blocked email) is later resolved.

findings.title: No tests for the migrated domain whitelist/blacklist validation logic
findings.body: This file now contains the domain whitelist/blacklist logic that used to live in `User#email_validator` (removed from `app/models/user.rb`), but `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb` only tests the new `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch. There is no test coverage in this PR for `email_domains_whitelist`/`email_domains_blacklist` behavior in its new location, so a regression in that migrated logic (e.g., broken regex construction, broken short-circuit ordering with the new blocked-email check) would go undetected.
